Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

vignette: John, a 67-year-old widowed interior designer of Oceania descent, has been grappling with the aftermath of a traumatic captivity experience. The event itself was deeply searing; John had been taken captive and subjected to constant shouting in Arabic by his captors. This trauma has left him with vivid, intrusive memories that resurface unexpectedly, often triggered by sounds or situations reminiscent of those harrowing days. John’s life has transformed dramatically since the event. He now meticulously rehearses conversations before any interaction, convinced that spontaneous speech might betray his fear and vulnerability. These rehearsal behaviors have extended to his work; he avoids going into client meetings or workshops where enclosed spaces remind him of his captivity. The avoidance behavior is not just about physical settings but also extends to social engagements, as John fears being trapped in situations similar to the ones during his captivity. One evening, while working on a design project at home, a distant noise—a car backfiring—triggered an intense flashback. He found himself suddenly reliving the shouting and fear from those days. This experience left him feeling emotionally vulnerable and heightened his sense of danger. Since then, John has become increasingly hypervigilant; he feels unsafe unless his back is against a wall where he can see everything around him. John’s memories of captivity are often emotionless or fragmented. He can recall the events, but they feel as if they happened to someone else, leaving him feeling numb. When he tries to recount what happened, he struggles to articulate the experience clearly, losing his train of thought midway through any attempt at explanation. The auditory aspect of these memories is particularly vivid; during flashbacks, John often hears the Arabic shouting in his head. This inability to fully process and explain his trauma has exacerbated his negative emotions such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame. He is certain that his body reacts to perceived danger before he can consciously think about it, further deepening his sense of vulnerability and hypervigilance. His maladaptive strategies, like rehearsing conversations and avoiding enclosed spaces, only serve to reinforce these negative emotions and the intrusive memories. John’s avoidance behavior at work has begun to affect his relationships with clients and colleagues. He has started missing important meetings and design presentations, leading to strained professional interactions. This occupational consequence is a significant source of anxiety for him; he worries that his performance and reliability are being questioned. What finally brought John to seek help was the realization that his strategies were not only failing but also making things worse. The intrusive memories and triggers have grown more frequent and intense, leaving him feeling trapped in a cycle of fear and avoidance. He is most afraid of losing control completely or becoming too dependent on these maladaptive behaviors. John hopes that through therapy, he can break free from the overwhelming sense of danger and find a way to process his traumatic experiences without being overwhelmed by them. His primary goal is to regain a sense of safety in his daily life and restore some normalcy to his work and personal interactions.
